bibl.title: Diagnostic criteria for persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD): Consensus document of the committee for the Classification of Vestibular Disorders of the Barany Society

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: A DIAGNOSIS CREATED BY MERGING FOUR OLDER TERMS RATHER THAN BY SPLITTING ONE - persistent postural-perceptual dizziness, assembled by the Barany Society from 30 years of research on phobic postural vertigo, space-motion discomfort, visual vertigo and chronic subjective dizziness, and written into the ICD-11 beta draft
span.quote: This paper presents diagnostic criteria for persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) to be included in the International Classification of Vestibular Disorders (ICVD). The term PPPD is new, but the disorder is not. Its diagnostic criteria were derived by expert consensus from an exhaustive review of 30 years of research on phobic postural vertigo, space-motion discomfort, visual vertigo, and chronic subjective dizziness.

span.label: what a clinician must find before calling chronic dizziness PPPD, when no examination, laboratory test or image is pathognomonic and the diagnosis is nonetheless not one of exclusion
span.quote: There are no findings on physical examination, laboratory testing, or diagnostic imaging that are pathognomonic of PPPD. Data from physical examinations and clinically indicated diagnostic testing help to determine if PPPD is the best diagnosis, either alone or in combination with other diseases or disorders (Criterion E). In this regard, an abnormal finding on physical examination or laboratory testing does not exclude a diagnosis of PPPD. Rather, when all criteria for PPPD are met, positive findings on examination or testing indicate the ongoing presence of a precipitating condition or another co-existing illness. Furthermore, PPPD is not a diagnosis of exclusion [ 12, 24, 75 ]. It should not be given to patients who report only non-specific chronic vestibular symptoms or those who have enigmatic complaints that do not fulfill its definition. In such cases, prospective monitoring may provide the clinical evidence needed to verify or exclude the diagnosis.

span.label: five diagnostic criteria A-E with seven explanatory notes, a differential diagnosis against nine named conditions, and a published account of where the committee's own consensus standard was not met
span.quote: PPPD is a chronic vestibular disorder defined by criteria A-E below. All five criteria must be fulfilled to make the diagnosis.

span.label: method
span.quote: The consensus process for decision-making seeks a result that has broad support. It does not require unanimity, but demands more than a simple majority [ 83 ]. Were the latter sufficient for developing diagnostic criteria or writing treatment guidelines, then informative aspects of the minority opinion could be lost to practicing clinicians, the scientific community, and general public. Though not all agree [ 44 ], arguments for publishing minority opinions in such endeavors have been made [ 56 ].

span.label: four terms coined in four clinical settings over three decades, describing overlapping patients, consolidated into one name whose precursors are kept as index terms in the classification that supersedes them
span.quote: In the absence of definitive scientific data on these possible subtypes, the Behavioral Subcommittee chose to define only PPPD for the ICVD, but allow for clinical variability as reflected in Criterion B. The World Health Organization permits related terms to be listed in the ICD-11. Therefore, PPV, SMD, VV, and CSD were retained as index terms for cross-referencing in the ICD-11 beta draft definition of PPPD [ 97 ].

span.label: an expert-consensus process with a stated decision rule - broad support, more than a simple majority, unanimity not required - iterated through four international meetings and a public posting, with the minority position printed
span.term: an expert-consensus process with a stated decision rule - broad support, more than a simple majority, unanimity not required - iterated through four international meetings and a public posting, with the minority position printed
span.quote: The consensus process for decision-making seeks a result that has broad support. It does not require unanimity, but demands more than a simple majority [ 83 ]. Were the latter sufficient for developing diagnostic criteria or writing treatment guidelines, then informative aspects of the minority opinion could be lost to practicing clinicians, the scientific community, and general public. Though not all agree [ 44 ], arguments for publishing minority opinions in such endeavors have been made [ 56 ].

span.label: **A DIAGNOSIS MADE BY CONSOLIDATION, WHICH IS A SHAPE THIS CORPUS DID NOT HAVE**: `THE TERM PPPD IS NEW, BUT THE DISORDER IS NOT. Its diagnostic criteria were DERIVED BY EXPERT CONSENSUS FROM AN EXHAUSTIVE REVIEW OF 30 YEARS OF RESEARCH ON PHOBIC POSTURAL VERTIGO, SPACE-MOTION DISCOMFORT, VISUAL VERTIGO, AND CHRONIC SUBJECTIVE DIZZINESS.` Every other naming event we hold splits, renames, retires or revises. **This one MERGES four terms from four clinical settings into one**
span.quote: This paper presents diagnostic criteria for persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) to be included in the International Classification of Vestibular Disorders (ICVD). The term PPPD is new, but the disorder is not. Its diagnostic criteria were derived by expert consensus from an exhaustive review of 30 years of research on phobic postural vertigo, space-motion discomfort, visual vertigo, and chronic subjective dizziness.

span.label: **AND THE BODY PUBLISHES ITS OWN DECISION RULE BEFORE REPORTING ANY DECISION**: `The consensus process for decision-making seeks a result that has broad support. IT DOES NOT REQUIRE UNANIMITY, BUT DEMANDS MORE THAN A SIMPLE MAJORITY. WERE THE LATTER SUFFICIENT for developing diagnostic criteria or writing treatment guidelines, THEN INFORMATIVE ASPECTS OF THE MINORITY OPINION COULD BE LOST to practicing clinicians, the scientific community, and general public.` The threshold is stated, and the reason for it is that a bare majority DISCARDS INFORMATION
span.quote: The consensus process for decision-making seeks a result that has broad support. It does not require unanimity, but demands more than a simple majority [ 83 ]. Were the latter sufficient for developing diagnostic criteria or writing treatment guidelines, then informative aspects of the minority opinion could be lost to practicing clinicians, the scientific community, and general public. Though not all agree [ 44 ], arguments for publishing minority opinions in such endeavors have been made [ 56 ].

span.label: **AND THEN IT NAMES THE SUB-QUESTION THAT FAILED THAT RULE**: `Members of the Behavioral Subcommittee and their advisors REACHED CONSENSUS about the diagnostic criteria for PPPD and its relationship to SMD, VV, and CSD, BUT NOT PPV.` The boundary of the agreement is published with the agreement - and the corpus has nothing else that draws it this precisely
span.quote: Members of the Behavioral Subcommittee and their advisors reached consensus about the diagnostic criteria for PPPD and its relationship to SMD, VV, and CSD, but not PPV. SMD and VV were seen as complex symptoms, not stand alone diagnostic entities. They informed criterion B of PPPD, but are known to occur in other situations as well [ 15, 39 ]. The definition of PPPD paralleled work in other areas of medicine where functional disorders (e.g., the functional gastrointestinal disorders [ 25, 91 ] and fibromyalgia [ 93, 94 ]) were defined by their core physical symptoms and not associated psychological features. CSD was a step in that direction based in part on the physical features of PPV [ 79 ]. However, the definition of PPPD is better supported; hence, PPPD now fully supplants CSD.

span.label: **AND THE VOTE ON THAT QUESTION IS RECORDED, AT A MAJORITY THE COMMITTEE'S OWN RULE CALLS INSUFFICIENT**: `IN THE END, A SIMPLE MAJORITY of subcommittee members VOTED AGAINST including PPV as a subtype of PPPD` - after two paragraphs printing the arguments in favour (30 years of research, personality and phobic factors that `affect clinical presentation`) and against (`DIFFICULT TO OPERATIONALIZE`, `MAY HAVE TO BE UPDATED`, `COULD PERPLEX CLINICIANS AND INVESTIGATORS`). **A body that says a simple majority is not enough, and then reports one**
span.quote: Members of the subcommittee and their advisors carefully considered a proposal to include PPV as a subtype of PPPD. Arguments in favor of this idea focused on the richness of the definition of PPV, which includes personality factors and psychological symptoms, particularly phobic symptoms, that were shown to affect clinical presentation [ 12, 71 ], as well as 30 years of research that described its clinical course [ 12, 35, 36 ] and identified potential pathophysiologic mechanisms [ 33, 46, 67, 68, 71, 98 ]. Arguments against the idea included concerns that the mix of physical and psychological symptoms and personality traits that constitute PPV is difficult to operationalize in clinical practice [ 75 ] and may have to be updated based on newer research [ 76, 85 ], and that including PPV as a subtype of PPPD without validating their relationship could perplex clinicians and investigators. In the end, a simple majority of subcommittee members voted against including PPV as a subtype of PPPD.

span.label: AND ONE AUTHOR'S OWN EARLIER DEFINITION IS RETIRED BY NAME IN THE SAME PARAGRAPH: `However, the definition of PPPD IS BETTER SUPPORTED; hence, PPPD NOW FULLY SUPPLANTS CSD.` Staab defined chronic subjective dizziness in 2004, defined it `MORE EXPLICITLY IN 2007`, and is the first author here
span.quote: Members of the Behavioral Subcommittee and their advisors reached consensus about the diagnostic criteria for PPPD and its relationship to SMD, VV, and CSD, but not PPV. SMD and VV were seen as complex symptoms, not stand alone diagnostic entities. They informed criterion B of PPPD, but are known to occur in other situations as well [ 15, 39 ]. The definition of PPPD paralleled work in other areas of medicine where functional disorders (e.g., the functional gastrointestinal disorders [ 25, 91 ] and fibromyalgia [ 93, 94 ]) were defined by their core physical symptoms and not associated psychological features. CSD was a step in that direction based in part on the physical features of PPV [ 79 ]. However, the definition of PPPD is better supported; hence, PPPD now fully supplants CSD.

span.label: **AND THE SUPERSEDED TERMS SURVIVE AS MACHINE-READABLE POINTERS**: `The World Health Organization permits related terms to be listed in the ICD-11. Therefore, PPV, SMD, VV, AND CSD WERE RETAINED AS INDEX TERMS FOR CROSS-REFERENCING in the ICD-11 beta draft definition of PPPD.` Our `alternatives` layer, in a real classification, decided by a committee - a retired name kept precisely so that the old literature still resolves
span.quote: In the absence of definitive scientific data on these possible subtypes, the Behavioral Subcommittee chose to define only PPPD for the ICVD, but allow for clinical variability as reflected in Criterion B. The World Health Organization permits related terms to be listed in the ICD-11. Therefore, PPV, SMD, VV, and CSD were retained as index terms for cross-referencing in the ICD-11 beta draft definition of PPPD [ 97 ].

span.label: **AND A CRITERION SET BY CONSENSUS IN THE ADMITTED ABSENCE OF ANY MEASUREMENT**: `THERE ARE NO DATA to identify one of these factors as being consistently more troublesome than the others OR TO DETERMINE THE SENSITIVITIES AND SPECIFICITIES OF REQUIRING THE PRESENCE OF ONE, TWO, OR ALL THREE FACTORS to make a diagnosis of PPPD. THEREFORE, the consensus definition of Criterion B REQUIRES that affected individuals report AT LEAST SOME DIFFICULTY WITH ALL THREE FACTORS.` The strictest of the three options, chosen BECAUSE none of them has been measured
span.quote: There are no data to identify one of these factors as being consistently more troublesome than the others or to determine the sensitivities and specificities of requiring the presence of one, two, or all three factors to make a diagnosis of PPPD. Therefore, the consensus definition of Criterion B requires that affected individuals report at least some difficulty with all three factors, while recognizing that patients will not be equally sensitive to all of them, and that the most troublesome of these factors will vary from one patient with PPPD to another.

span.label: **AND A WORD TAKEN BACK FROM ITS OWN TWENTIETH-CENTURY SENSE**: `Here FUNCTIONAL conditions are considered AS THEY WERE IN THE EARLY 19TH CENTURY as disorders `arising from a change in the mode of action of an organ`, unrelated to structural or cellular deficits ... IN THIS CONNOTATION, FUNCTIONAL IS NOT A SYNONYM FOR PSYCHOGENIC OR PSYCHOSOMATIC AS IT WAS THROUGHOUT MOST OF THE 20TH CENTURY.` A definition reverting a term to an older sense **and naming the sense it rejects**
span.quote: Here functional conditions are considered as they were in the early 19th century as disorders “arising from a change in the mode of action of an organ” [ 20 ], unrelated to structural or cellular deficits. As revived in the modern era, most notably in gastroenterology [ 25 ], this concept of functional conditions distinguishes them from psychiatric illnesses. In this connotation, functional is not a synonym for psychogenic or psychosomatic as it was throughout most of the 20th century and, therefore, does not reflect a presumption of psychopathological abnormalities.

span.label: AND THE SOCIETY'S OWN CURRENT TERM IS SET ASIDE, DELIBERATELY AND WITH A REASON: `In 2009, THE BARANY SOCIETY ADOPTED THE TERM VISUALLY INDUCED DIZZINESS OR VID TO REPLACE VV in the ICVD nomenclature ... HEREIN, THE HISTORICAL MONIKER VV IS USED to refer to Bronstein's original description and the subsequent body of research on that symptom.` A paper knowingly using a superseded term, because the LITERATURE it is summarising is indexed under the old one
span.quote: In 2009, the Bárány Society adopted the term visually induced dizziness or VID to replace VV in the ICVD nomenclature for vestibular symptoms [ 9 ]. Herein, the historical moniker VV is used to refer to Bronstein’s original description and the subsequent body of research on that symptom.

span.label: AND A PRECEDENT FOR WHAT HAPPENS WHEN NOBODY DOES THIS: `As otology, neurology, and psychiatry MATURED INTO SEPARATE SPECIALTIES in the early 20th century, PLATZSCHWINDEL AND PLATZANGST FADED FROM USE and AGORAPHOBIA BECAME A PSYCHIATRIC DISORDER, LOSING ITS SPACE AND MOTION CONTEXT.` Two terms died and a third survived with **part of its meaning removed** - not by decision, by disciplinary drift. The 1870s syndromes and PPPD describe the same patients
span.quote: As otology, neurology, and psychiatry matured into separate specialties in the early 20th century, Platzschwindel and Platzangst faded from use and agoraphobia became a psychiatric disorder, losing its space and motion context [ 3, 95 ].

span.label: AND THE DEFINERS WARN AGAINST READING THEIR OWN CRITERIA AS A CHECKLIST: `Clinicians who apply Criteria A and B AS SIMPLE CHECKLISTS of symptoms WITHOUT CAPTURING THE DYNAMIC FEATURES of their patients' histories (Criterion C) ASSUME A REDUCTIONIST VIEW of the diagnosis ... Scientists who fail to consider the dynamics of PPPD RISK MUDDLING RATHER THAN ILLUMINATING the nature of the disorder.` The instrument comes with an instruction not to use it as an instrument
span.quote: The debate about PPV highlighted the fact that PPPD is a dynamic condition as illustrated in Fig. 1 . It is a functional disorder, although structural and psychological factors affect its development. Clinicians who apply Criteria A and B as simple checklists of symptoms without capturing the dynamic features of their patients’ histories (Criterion C) assume a reductionist view of the diagnosis, potentially missing important aspects of patients’ morbidity (Criterion D) and nuances of the differential diagnosis (Criterion E). Scientists who fail to consider the dynamics of PPPD risk muddling rather than illuminating the nature of the disorder and its pathophysiologic mechanisms.

span.label: **NO POSITIVE TEST, AND NOT A DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION EITHER**: `THERE ARE NO FINDINGS ON PHYSICAL EXAMINATION, LABORATORY TESTING, OR DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING THAT ARE PATHOGNOMONIC OF PPPD ... an ABNORMAL finding on physical examination or laboratory testing DOES NOT EXCLUDE a diagnosis of PPPD ... Furthermore, PPPD IS NOT A DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION.` Both doors are shut: nothing confirms it and nothing rules it out, and it may not be given by elimination either
span.quote: There are no findings on physical examination, laboratory testing, or diagnostic imaging that are pathognomonic of PPPD. Data from physical examinations and clinically indicated diagnostic testing help to determine if PPPD is the best diagnosis, either alone or in combination with other diseases or disorders (Criterion E). In this regard, an abnormal finding on physical examination or laboratory testing does not exclude a diagnosis of PPPD. Rather, when all criteria for PPPD are met, positive findings on examination or testing indicate the ongoing presence of a precipitating condition or another co-existing illness. Furthermore, PPPD is not a diagnosis of exclusion [ 12, 24, 75 ]. It should not be given to patients who report only non-specific chronic vestibular symptoms or those who have enigmatic complaints that do not fulfill its definition. In such cases, prospective monitoring may provide the clinical evidence needed to verify or exclude the diagnosis.

span.label: AND WHETHER IT IS ONE DISORDER AT ALL IS PRINTED AS AN OPEN QUESTION: `(a) IS PPPD A SINGLE DISORDER with one principal pathophysiologic process OR IS IT THE COMMON MANIFESTATION OF MULTIPLE CONDITIONS that produce similar symptoms from different pathophysiologic mechanisms? (b) If PPPD is a single disorder, DOES IT HAVE clinically meaningful and VALIDLY DISTINGUISHABLE SUBTYPES?` Two analogies are offered for the two answers - PTSD for one syndrome from many precipitants, hypertension for one number from many diseases
span.quote: The current state of scientific knowledge left two important questions unanswered: (a) Is PPPD a single disorder with one principal pathophysiologic process or is it the common manifestation of multiple conditions that produce similar symptoms from different pathophysiologic mechanisms? (b) If PPPD is a single disorder, does it have clinically meaningful and validly distinguishable subtypes?

span.label: AND A SUBTHRESHOLD CATEGORY WAS REFUSED FOR WANT OF DATA: `Members of the subcommittee concluded that THERE WERE NOT ENOUGH PUBLISHED DATA TO DEFINE a clinically meaningful PROBABLE OR SUBTHRESHOLD version of PPPD.` The Barany Society's own vestibular migraine and Meniere criteria carry `probable` tiers; this one declines to, and says why
span.quote: Members of the subcommittee concluded that there were not enough published data to define a clinically meaningful probable or subthreshold version of PPPD. Clinical experience with PPV and CSD suggests caution in applying the diagnosis of PPPD to patients who do not fulfill all five of its diagnostic criteria.

span.label: AND THE EPIDEMIOLOGY IS BORROWED FROM THE FOUR PRECURSORS, NOT MEASURED ON PPPD: `No epidemiologic studies are available for PPPD, but ITS PREVALENCE AND INCIDENCE MAY BE ESTIMATED FROM RESEARCH DONE ON PATIENTS WITH PPV, VV, CSD` - so every frequency in this paper describes populations defined by the terms PPPD replaces
span.quote: Clinical epidemiologic data from tertiary care centers with special interest in PPV [ 13 ] and CSD [ 79 ] showed their prevalence to be 15–20% among all patients presenting for evaluation of vestibular symptoms, making them the most common diagnoses among young adults and the second most common among all adults, trailing only BPPV. The average duration of illness at the time of tertiary consultation was 4.5 years with some patients experiencing symptoms for decades [ 13, 79 ].

span.label: requiring ALL FIVE criteria A-E, and declining to publish a `probable` or subthreshold tier for patients who meet only some
span.note: eliminates: applying the label to non-specific chronic dizziness - which the paper warns against in the same breath as saying PPPD is NOT a diagnosis of exclusion · outcome: held
span.quote: Members of the subcommittee concluded that there were not enough published data to define a clinically meaningful probable or subthreshold version of PPPD. Clinical experience with PPV and CSD suggests caution in applying the diagnosis of PPPD to patients who do not fulfill all five of its diagnostic criteria.

span.label: requiring at least some difficulty with ALL THREE exacerbating factors of Criterion B, rather than one or two
span.note: eliminates: nothing that has been measured - the paper states outright that the sensitivities and specificities of the one-, two- and three-factor rules are unknown · outcome: partial

span.label: a period of prospective monitoring with a symptom log and serial examinations when no precipitant can be identified or symptoms worsen gradually
span.note: eliminates: mistaking a slowly emerging degenerative disorder for PPPD · outcome: held
span.quote: There are no findings on physical examination, laboratory testing, or diagnostic imaging that are pathognomonic of PPPD. Data from physical examinations and clinically indicated diagnostic testing help to determine if PPPD is the best diagnosis, either alone or in combination with other diseases or disorders (Criterion E). In this regard, an abnormal finding on physical examination or laboratory testing does not exclude a diagnosis of PPPD. Rather, when all criteria for PPPD are met, positive findings on examination or testing indicate the ongoing presence of a precipitating condition or another co-existing illness. Furthermore, PPPD is not a diagnosis of exclusion [ 12, 24, 75 ]. It should not be given to patients who report only non-specific chronic vestibular symptoms or those who have enigmatic complaints that do not fulfill its definition. In such cases, prospective monitoring may provide the clinical evidence needed to verify or exclude the diagnosis.

span.label: anxiety disorders
span.quote: Patients with PPPD may express concerns about having to endure increases in their noxious symptoms on exposure to exacerbating factors, but this differs from individuals with anxiety disorders who focus more on fears of becoming incapacitated, injuring themselves or others, or attracting unwanted attention when exposed to situations that they fear.

span.label: MdDS
span.quote: A major difference between MdDS and PPPD is the extent of treatment response. MdDS generally has a limited response to vestibular habituation exercises or medications, whereas treatment studies of PPV [ 86 ], SMD [ 42, 92 ], VV [ 62, 64 ], CSD [ 81 ], and PPPD, itself [ 84 ], showed significant improvements with vestibular habituation or serotonergic antidepressants.

ALL FIVE CRITERIA MUST BE FULFILLED TO MAKE THE DIAGNOSIS.` The ICVD divides by DURATION (acute / episodic / chronic) and by PRESUMED MECHANISM (structural / functional / psychiatric), and PPPD is chronic-functional on both

Its diagnostic criteria were derived by expert consensus from an exhaustive review of 30 years of research on phobic postural vertigo, space-motion discomfort, visual vertigo, and chronic subjective dizziness.

span.note: the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.95 — `IN 2009, THE BARANY SOCIETY ADOPTED THE TERM VISUALLY INDUCED DIZZINESS OR VID TO REPLACE VV IN THE ICVD NOMENCLATURE for vestibular symptoms. HEREIN, THE HISTORICAL MONIKER VV IS USED to refer to Bronstein's original description and the subsequent body of research on that symptom.` The rename is real and eight years old; the authors set it aside because THE EVIDENCE THEY ARE SUMMARISING IS INDEXED UNDER THE OLD NAME. A retired term still doing work, in the same paper that retires CSD
span.quote: In 2009, the Bárány Society adopted the term visually induced dizziness or VID to replace VV in the ICVD nomenclature for vestibular symptoms [ 9 ]. Herein, the historical moniker VV is used to refer to Bronstein’s original description and the subsequent body of research on that symptom.

span.label: functional —distinct-from→ psychogenic
span.note: the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.95 — `IN THIS CONNOTATION, FUNCTIONAL IS NOT A SYNONYM FOR PSYCHOGENIC OR PSYCHOSOMATIC AS IT WAS THROUGHOUT MOST OF THE 20TH CENTURY and, therefore, DOES NOT REFLECT A PRESUMPTION OF PSYCHOPATHOLOGICAL ABNORMALITIES.` The edge records a term being pulled back from a sense it held for eighty years - and the paper dates both senses and cites the field (gastroenterology) that revived the older one
span.quote: Here functional conditions are considered as they were in the early 19th century as disorders “arising from a change in the mode of action of an organ” [ 20 ], unrelated to structural or cellular deficits. As revived in the modern era, most notably in gastroenterology [ 25 ], this concept of functional conditions distinguishes them from psychiatric illnesses. In this connotation, functional is not a synonym for psychogenic or psychosomatic as it was throughout most of the 20th century and, therefore, does not reflect a presumption of psychopathological abnormalities.

span.label: PPPD —distinct-from→ anxiety disorders
span.note: the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.95 — `Patients with PPPD may express concerns about having to ENDURE INCREASES IN THEIR NOXIOUS SYMPTOMS on exposure to exacerbating factors, BUT THIS DIFFERS FROM INDIVIDUALS WITH ANXIETY DISORDERS WHO FOCUS MORE ON FEARS of becoming incapacitated, injuring themselves or others, or attracting unwanted attention.` The two conditions are separated by WHAT THE PATIENT IS AFRAID OF - a distinction with no test behind it, in a paper that says no test exists
span.quote: Patients with PPPD may express concerns about having to endure increases in their noxious symptoms on exposure to exacerbating factors, but this differs from individuals with anxiety disorders who focus more on fears of becoming incapacitated, injuring themselves or others, or attracting unwanted attention when exposed to situations that they fear.

span.label: MdDS —distinct-from→ PPPD
span.note: the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.95 — `A MAJOR DIFFERENCE BETWEEN MdDS AND PPPD IS THE EXTENT OF TREATMENT RESPONSE. MdDS generally has A LIMITED RESPONSE to vestibular habituation exercises or medications, WHEREAS treatment studies of PPV, SMD, VV, CSD, and PPPD, itself, SHOWED SIGNIFICANT IMPROVEMENTS.` **A boundary drawn by what the patients do after treatment**, in a corpus where boundaries are usually drawn by a marker or a cut-off
span.quote: A major difference between MdDS and PPPD is the extent of treatment response. MdDS generally has a limited response to vestibular habituation exercises or medications, whereas treatment studies of PPV [ 86 ], SMD [ 42, 92 ], VV [ 62, 64 ], CSD [ 81 ], and PPPD, itself [ 84 ], showed significant improvements with vestibular habituation or serotonergic antidepressants.

span.label: **A DIAGNOSIS MADE BY CONSOLIDATING FOUR OLDER TERMS**: `THE TERM PPPD IS NEW, BUT THE DISORDER IS NOT ... derived ... from an exhaustive review of 30 YEARS OF RESEARCH ON phobic postural vertigo, space-motion discomfort, visual vertigo, and chronic subjective dizziness`
span.term: **A DIAGNOSIS MADE BY CONSOLIDATING FOUR OLDER TERMS**: `THE TERM PPPD IS NEW, BUT THE DISORDER IS NOT ... derived ... from an exhaustive review of 30 YEARS OF RESEARCH ON phobic postural vertigo, space-motion discomfort, visual vertigo, and chronic subjective dizziness`
span.quote: This paper presents diagnostic criteria for persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) to be included in the International Classification of Vestibular Disorders (ICVD). The term PPPD is new, but the disorder is not. Its diagnostic criteria were derived by expert consensus from an exhaustive review of 30 years of research on phobic postural vertigo, space-motion discomfort, visual vertigo, and chronic subjective dizziness.

span.label: **AND A COMMITTEE THAT PUBLISHES ITS OWN DECISION RULE**: `It DOES NOT REQUIRE UNANIMITY, BUT DEMANDS MORE THAN A SIMPLE MAJORITY` - because otherwise `INFORMATIVE ASPECTS OF THE MINORITY OPINION COULD BE LOST`
span.term: **AND A COMMITTEE THAT PUBLISHES ITS OWN DECISION RULE**: `It DOES NOT REQUIRE UNANIMITY, BUT DEMANDS MORE THAN A SIMPLE MAJORITY` - because otherwise `INFORMATIVE ASPECTS OF THE MINORITY OPINION COULD BE LOST`
span.quote: The consensus process for decision-making seeks a result that has broad support. It does not require unanimity, but demands more than a simple majority [ 83 ]. Were the latter sufficient for developing diagnostic criteria or writing treatment guidelines, then informative aspects of the minority opinion could be lost to practicing clinicians, the scientific community, and general public. Though not all agree [ 44 ], arguments for publishing minority opinions in such endeavors have been made [ 56 ].

span.label: **AND THEN REPORTS A DECISION TAKEN AT EXACTLY THE MAJORITY IT CALLS INSUFFICIENT**: `IN THE END, A SIMPLE MAJORITY of subcommittee members VOTED AGAINST including PPV as a subtype of PPPD` - and `reached consensus ... BUT NOT PPV`
span.term: **AND THEN REPORTS A DECISION TAKEN AT EXACTLY THE MAJORITY IT CALLS INSUFFICIENT**: `IN THE END, A SIMPLE MAJORITY of subcommittee members VOTED AGAINST including PPV as a subtype of PPPD` - and `reached consensus ... BUT NOT PPV`
span.quote: Members of the subcommittee and their advisors carefully considered a proposal to include PPV as a subtype of PPPD. Arguments in favor of this idea focused on the richness of the definition of PPV, which includes personality factors and psychological symptoms, particularly phobic symptoms, that were shown to affect clinical presentation [ 12, 71 ], as well as 30 years of research that described its clinical course [ 12, 35, 36 ] and identified potential pathophysiologic mechanisms [ 33, 46, 67, 68, 71, 98 ]. Arguments against the idea included concerns that the mix of physical and psychological symptoms and personality traits that constitute PPV is difficult to operationalize in clinical practice [ 75 ] and may have to be updated based on newer research [ 76, 85 ], and that including PPV as a subtype of PPPD without validating their relationship could perplex clinicians and investigators. In the end, a simple majority of subcommittee members voted against including PPV as a subtype of PPPD.

span.label: AND THE RETIRED TERMS ARE KEPT AS MACHINE-READABLE POINTERS: `PPV, SMD, VV, AND CSD WERE RETAINED AS INDEX TERMS FOR CROSS-REFERENCING in the ICD-11 beta draft definition of PPPD`
span.term: AND THE RETIRED TERMS ARE KEPT AS MACHINE-READABLE POINTERS: `PPV, SMD, VV, AND CSD WERE RETAINED AS INDEX TERMS FOR CROSS-REFERENCING in the ICD-11 beta draft definition of PPPD`
span.quote: In the absence of definitive scientific data on these possible subtypes, the Behavioral Subcommittee chose to define only PPPD for the ICVD, but allow for clinical variability as reflected in Criterion B. The World Health Organization permits related terms to be listed in the ICD-11. Therefore, PPV, SMD, VV, and CSD were retained as index terms for cross-referencing in the ICD-11 beta draft definition of PPPD [ 97 ].

span.label: AND A CRITERION SET IN THE ADMITTED ABSENCE OF MEASUREMENT: `THERE ARE NO DATA ... to determine the SENSITIVITIES AND SPECIFICITIES of requiring the presence of ONE, TWO, OR ALL THREE FACTORS ... THEREFORE, the consensus definition of Criterion B requires ... ALL THREE`
span.term: AND A CRITERION SET IN THE ADMITTED ABSENCE OF MEASUREMENT: `THERE ARE NO DATA ... to determine the SENSITIVITIES AND SPECIFICITIES of requiring the presence of ONE, TWO, OR ALL THREE FACTORS ... THEREFORE, the consensus definition of Criterion B requires ... ALL THREE`
span.quote: There are no data to identify one of these factors as being consistently more troublesome than the others or to determine the sensitivities and specificities of requiring the presence of one, two, or all three factors to make a diagnosis of PPPD. Therefore, the consensus definition of Criterion B requires that affected individuals report at least some difficulty with all three factors, while recognizing that patients will not be equally sensitive to all of them, and that the most troublesome of these factors will vary from one patient with PPPD to another.

span.label: AND A WORD PULLED BACK FROM ITS OWN 20TH-CENTURY SENSE: `functional IS NOT A SYNONYM FOR PSYCHOGENIC OR PSYCHOSOMATIC AS IT WAS THROUGHOUT MOST OF THE 20TH CENTURY`
span.term: AND A WORD PULLED BACK FROM ITS OWN 20TH-CENTURY SENSE: `functional IS NOT A SYNONYM FOR PSYCHOGENIC OR PSYCHOSOMATIC AS IT WAS THROUGHOUT MOST OF THE 20TH CENTURY`
span.quote: Here functional conditions are considered as they were in the early 19th century as disorders “arising from a change in the mode of action of an organ” [ 20 ], unrelated to structural or cellular deficits. As revived in the modern era, most notably in gastroenterology [ 25 ], this concept of functional conditions distinguishes them from psychiatric illnesses. In this connotation, functional is not a synonym for psychogenic or psychosomatic as it was throughout most of the 20th century and, therefore, does not reflect a presumption of psychopathological abnormalities.

span.label: AND A TERM THAT SURVIVED BY LOSING PART OF ITS MEANING: `Platzschwindel and Platzangst FADED FROM USE and AGORAPHOBIA BECAME A PSYCHIATRIC DISORDER, LOSING ITS SPACE AND MOTION CONTEXT` - drift, not decision
span.term: AND A TERM THAT SURVIVED BY LOSING PART OF ITS MEANING: `Platzschwindel and Platzangst FADED FROM USE and AGORAPHOBIA BECAME A PSYCHIATRIC DISORDER, LOSING ITS SPACE AND MOTION CONTEXT` - drift, not decision
span.quote: As otology, neurology, and psychiatry matured into separate specialties in the early 20th century, Platzschwindel and Platzangst faded from use and agoraphobia became a psychiatric disorder, losing its space and motion context [ 3, 95 ].

span.label: `A CHRONIC VESTIBULAR DISORDER DEFINED BY CRITERIA A-E ... ALL FIVE CRITERIA MUST BE FULFILLED` - one or more of dizziness, unsteadiness or non-spinning vertigo on most days for 3 months or more, exacerbated by upright posture, active or passive motion, and moving or complex visual stimuli
span.quote: PPPD is a chronic vestibular disorder defined by criteria A-E below. All five criteria must be fulfilled to make the diagnosis.

span.label: `disorders ARISING FROM A CHANGE IN THE MODE OF ACTION OF AN ORGAN, unrelated to structural or cellular deficits` - the early-19th-century sense, revived in gastroenterology, explicitly NOT the 20th-century psychogenic sense
span.quote: Here functional conditions are considered as they were in the early 19th century as disorders “arising from a change in the mode of action of an organ” [ 20 ], unrelated to structural or cellular deficits. As revived in the modern era, most notably in gastroenterology [ 25 ], this concept of functional conditions distinguishes them from psychiatric illnesses. In this connotation, functional is not a synonym for psychogenic or psychosomatic as it was throughout most of the 20th century and, therefore, does not reflect a presumption of psychopathological abnormalities.

span.label: `Symptoms must be present for more than 15 of every 30 days. MOST AFFECTED INDIVIDUALS EXPERIENCE SYMPTOMS EVERY DAY OR NEARLY EVERY DAY` - the threshold is far below where the patients actually sit
span.quote: (2) Symptoms must be present for more than 15 of every 30 days. Most affected individuals experience symptoms every day or nearly every day. Symptoms tend to increase as the day progresses.

span.label: `making them THE MOST COMMON DIAGNOSES AMONG YOUNG ADULTS and the second most common among all adults, TRAILING ONLY BPPV`
span.term: prevalence of the precursor diagnoses in tertiary vestibular clinics
span.quote: Clinical epidemiologic data from tertiary care centers with special interest in PPV [ 13 ] and CSD [ 79 ] showed their prevalence to be 15–20% among all patients presenting for evaluation of vestibular symptoms, making them the most common diagnoses among young adults and the second most common among all adults, trailing only BPPV. The average duration of illness at the time of tertiary consultation was 4.5 years with some patients experiencing symptoms for decades [ 13, 79 ].

span.label: `These results indicate that PPPD IS LIKELY TO DEVELOP IN A SIGNIFICANT PROPORTION of patients afflicted with acute or episodic vestibular syndromes`
span.term: incidence after an acute or episodic vestibular disorder
span.quote: These investigations found PPPD-like chronic dizziness [ 7, 28, 30 ] or persistent VV [ 23 ] in about 25% of patients after 3–12 months of follow-up, despite otherwise adequate compensation or recovery from the initial illnesses. These results indicate that PPPD is likely to develop in a significant proportion of patients afflicted with acute or episodic vestibular syndromes.

span.label: the precipitant is part of Criterion C, and this is the only place its distribution is given
span.term: precipitating conditions, by share of cases
span.quote: The most common precipitating conditions are peripheral or central vestibular disorders (25–30% of cases), attacks of vestibular migraine (15–20%), panic attacks or anxiety that manifest prominent dizziness (15% each), concussive injuries of the brain or whiplash injuries of the neck (10–15%), and autonomic disorders (7%). Other conditions that are capable of producing vertigo, unsteadiness or dizziness, or altering balance function (e.g., cardiac dysrhythmias, adverse drug reactions) precipitate the disorder less commonly (collectively ∼3%) [ 74, 79 ].

span.label: `Staab, et al. found that THIS DIAGNOSTIC DEFINITION WAS HIGHLY SENSITIVE (>85%) AND SPECIFIC (>90%) FOR DETECTING CSD` - CSD, not PPPD. **The new definition supplants the old one on the strength of numbers measured on the old one**, and the paper says elsewhere that the sensitivities of its own Criterion B are unknown
span.term: the only sensitivity and specificity in the paper belong to the SUPPLANTED term
span.quote: Staab, et al. [ 74 ] found that this diagnostic definition was highly sensitive (>85%) and specific (>90%) for detecting CSD versus Menière’s disease, vestibular migraine, or benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), in patients with or without additional neuro-otologic comorbidity.

Therefore, the consensus definition of Criterion B requires that affected individuals report at least some difficulty with all three factors, while recognizing that patients will not be equally sensitive to all of them, and that the most troublesome of these factors will vary from one patient with PPPD to another.
